title: Move assets to S3
body:
We are moving all file uploads and static assets out of `priv/static` and on to S3. This branch includes all chages necessary to make that transition and shouldn't be merged until it's been tested in a production sandbox.

New environment variables:

- `AWS_REGION` - likely `us-east-1`
- `AWS_ASSETS_BUCKET` - tells Waffle where to upload files
- `AWS_UPLOADS_HOST` - tells Waffle which host to use for generating uploaded file URLs

_(I tried using separate AWS credentials for UPLOADS vs STATS, but because Waffle uses ExAws like our stats analyzer does, this became troublesome.)_

Things we still need:

- [x] A process to mirror/sync current uploads to the production S3 bucket
- [x] A `cdn.changelog.com` origin in Fastly that points to the production S3 bucket
- [x] A build step that takes compiled assets and uploads them to S3 on deploy

title: 🎁 Auto-restoring K8s clusters
body:
## Why did we do this?
- No ClickOps - 🙌🏻   @hasheddan - or TerminalOps for our K8s clusters
- We want to tell what we want via a K8s API, and have "the system" figure out how to talk to the IaaS
- If one of us accidentally deletes it, the cluster should be automatically re-created (the intent is in the title)

> 💡 This idea actually started in [Ship It #15 - Assemble all your infrastructure](https://changelog.com/shipit/15), where I was mentioning that we want to make Crossplane part of the Changelog 2022 setup.      
                                                                              
## How did we do this?

We created a new Crossplane provider for Linode using [Terrajet](https://github.com/crossplane/terrajet), a framework for generating Crossplane providers from Terraform providers. This is the end-result: [crossplane-contrib/provider-jet-linode](https://github.com/crossplane-contrib/provider-jet-linode)

These are all the steps, from start to finish:

### 1/5. Install Crossplane
```console
make lke-crossplane
Installing Crossplane v1.6.1...
helm upgrade crossplane crossplane-stable/crossplane \
	--install \
	--namespace crossplane-system --create-namespace \
	--version 1.6.1 \
	--wait
✅ Crossplane v1.6.1 installed!
```

### 2/5. Install  Linode Crossplane Provider
```console
make crossplane-linode-provider
Adding Linode Token...
Installing Crossplane Provider Linode vv0.0.0-12.ge4dcf7e...
Configuring Crossplane Provider Linode...
✅ Crossplane Provider Linode vv0.0.0-12.ge4dcf7e installed!
```

### 3/5. Provision LKE cluster with Provider
```console
export CROSSPLANE_LKE_NAME=lke-2021-12-24
make crossplane-lke
Creating lke-2021-12-24 running K8s v1.22 in us-east ...
✅ lke-2021-12-24 running K8s v1.22 in us-east with 1 worker node(s) of type g6-dedicated-8 created!
```

### 4/5. Target LKE cluster
```console
make crossplane-lke-kubeconfig
Saving lke-2021-12-24 LKE cluster config to /Users/gerhard/github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/2021/.config/kube/configs/lke-2021-12-24.yml...

✅ To use this config, run export KUBECONFIG=/Users/gerhard/github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/2021/.config/kube/configs/lke-2021-12-24.yml

export KUBECONFIG=/Users/gerhard/github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/2021/.config/kube/configs/lke-2021-12-24.yml
make k9s
```

> 💡 The worker node can take up to 5 minutes to get ready after the cluster becomes ready.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/149632113-d45ab10f-dbba-4a24-8f22-766f15a13167.png)

### 5/5. What happens if someone "accidentally" deletes a cluster? 😎
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/149631543-63b0c7c6-db8e-44b2-b8e5-faddd87e7813.png)

Within 1 minute, Crossplane Linode Provider notices that the cluster is missing. 1 minute later, the cluster gets re-created. After another 2 minutes, the worker node appears as not ready. After 1 more minute, the worker node becomes ready. All put together, the cluster will be re-created within 5 minutes of it getting "accidentally" deleted. 🙌🏻                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                     
## What happens next?
- [x] Run Crossplane & Linode Provider to Upbound Cloud
  - [x] Delete existing LKE cluster if using the same name, otherwise it will fail to create https://github.com/crossplane-contrib/provider-jet-linode/issues/6
  - [x] `make up-connect`
  - [x] `export KUBECONFIG=/Users/gerhard/github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/2021/.config/upbound.d9a7a122-fafe-4c06-a170-d0ad543f371c.yml` 
  - [x] `export CROSSPLANE_NAMESPACE=upbound-system`
  - [x] `export CROSSPLANE_LKE_NAME=lke-2021-12-24`
  - [x] `export CROSSPLANE_RUNNING_IN=upbound-2022`
  - [x] `export CROSSPLANE_VERSION=1.5.1-up.1`
  - [x] `make crossplane-lke`
- [ ] Tag [crossplane-contrib/provider-jet-linode](https://github.com/crossplane-contrib/provider-jet-linode)
- [ ] Check that https://doc.crds.dev/X gets populated after tagging

## And after that?

- Install everything that is needed on the LKE cluster using a Composition
  - base composition:
    - grafana-agent (sed + envsubst + kubectl)
    - honeycomb-agent (helm)
    - metrics-server (curl + gsed + kubectl)
    - external-dns (envsubst + kubectl)
    - cert-manager (helm)
    - ingress-nginx (helm)
    - local-path-provisioner (helm)
    - keel (helm)
  - changelog composition (envsubst + kubectl)
---

cc @muvaf @hasheddan @jbw976

title: 🎁 Continuous CPU profiling
body:
## Why did we do this?
* To understand how our K8s worker nodes use CPU
* To quickly generate and compare CPU profiles
* To look at the CPU profile from a longer-term perspective (hours)

## How did we do it?

We installed Parca agent first, and server next in our Kubernetes production cluster.
This is what that looks like:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/147135936-f0996881-39d9-4861-89d1-076fe3c43c09.png)

Next, we port-forward 7070 to Parca server, and load the UI:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/147136648-79babf1c-fd57-4cda-b543-f1a86cdc9e49.png)

We select **CPU Samples** profile, hit **Search** and see all workloads that use CPU across the K8s cluster:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/147136775-a0373370-eefe-4d61-b861-d18aa113287e.png)

Let's click on the process which has the most samples (this will be the one that uses the most CPU):

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/147136933-3e18aa1e-81f5-4e8b-932b-a22345889b15.png)

Great! We notice that this is the Parca (server), and we instantly see that widest span is actually symbolizing DWARF information. Is this a good thing or a bad thing? I mean, **I think** that it does what it's supposed to, but what I really want to do is compare a high number of samples, like this peak, to a low number of samples and try to understand what is different.

I hold `SHIFT`, click on the `container="parca"` label, then click the **Compare** button. Next, I click on a point in the graph with fewer samples on the left-hand side, and a point with a high number on the right-hand side. This is what I see:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/147138724-d00a779a-ebd4-4823-878f-46aadf989125.png)

> ASIDE: I know, this looks a lot like Christmas 🎄

All new spans on the right-hand side are shown as red, which means all that extra work that the CPU needs to do. I quickly spot that memory garbage collection makes for most of the new samples. My understanding is that this is due to the Parca server writing the CPU samples that it tracks to its storage, which is what happens just before garbage collection. This makes sense, and is exactly what I would expect to see when a process has "work" to do:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/147138575-82e33c68-027e-411a-b321-a0dc68ccfaad.png)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/147138280-5a30ceb7-9314-40ab-ade0-ed3c709766be.png)

That is already helpful, meaning that if I had to optimise something, since those functions use the most CPU, that's where I would start. Now remember, some of this may be necessary - after all, processes are meant to do work, and use CPU - but maybe they are not as efficient as they could be, and since those functions use the most CPU, I would need to go through that code and see what could be optimised or removed (if anything!).

The last thing that I want to mention regarding the **Compare** view is that:
- 💚  Green means less CPU activity
- 💙  Blue means the same amount of CPU activity
- ❤️  Red means more CPU activity

Lastly, if I wanted to see CPU profiles across everything for the last day perhaps (this may use a lot of memory!) I select **Last day** from the drop-down and click on the **Merge** button. This is what I see:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/147161191-7d2815b1-98a5-4708-beb9-0171db8ab5a0.png)

You will spot `postgres`, `calico` and almost half of all CPU spans in `parca`. The memory addresses on the left-hand side in the screenshot above are actually for the Erlang VM, which cannot be currently symbolized. This is a present in the sense that it's a missing feature and we are making the wider community aware of it. It would be amazing if we could understand what actually happens in the Erlang VM (the changelog.com app runtime - it's a [Phoenix app](https://www.phoenixframework.org/) fwiw) from a CPU perspective with eBPF & pprof (which is what Parca uses under the hood). If we were to use Parca to look at it today (v0.6.1), this is what we would see:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/147161632-065f4867-442d-4673-9f2a-731e8f72b28a.png)

To analyse a profile locally, click on **Download pprof** to download locally, uncompress, and then run the following command:

```sh
perf report -i /tmp/perf.data

# For time spent in each function without its children:
perf report --no-children -i /tmp/perf.data
```

## Anything else to add?

**By default, Parca server deploy does not have any CPU or memory limits.**

In the current implementation - `v0.6.1` - Parca server will OOM and restart when it reaches the memory limit. When this happens, all CPU samples will be lost. This is OK for us, even in production, and we simply patch the K8s deployment with CPU & memory limits.

## What happens next?

- [x] Listen to @brancz tell us more about this in [Ship It! #33](https://changelog.com/shipit/33)
- [x] Give feedback re missing PostgreSQL symbolisation. This was helpful:  [debuginfod](https://wiki.debian.org/Debuginfod)
- [x] Put Erlang / Elixir onto @brancz's radar
- [ ] Start a conversation in the Erlang / Elixir community re answering some of @brancz questions. Off the top of my head, I am thinking: @garazdawi @mkuratczyk @lawik @akoutmos @deadtrickster @ferd. FWIW, this was helpful: [Performance testing the JIT compiler for the BEAM VM](https://www.erlang-solutions.com/blog/performance-testing-the-jit-compiler-for-the-beam-vm/#profiling)

## Should I read the comments below?

If you are curious about the steps that went into this, have a look, otherwise all the important details are above the fold, meaning in this top-level comment. This is it for now, have a great Christmas 2021 🎄

---

As for the **one more thing** moment, I want to mention actually three things:

1. https://github.com/pyrra-dev/pyrra & https://demo.pyrra.dev/

2. https://github.com/parca-dev/parca-agent/blob/0327839ff8d58042c27f7588e61c73cba4b5b3b3/Dockerfile

Notice how Parca pins the apt sources, and then installs the packes with no versions, since the sources pin them. This is the best way to ensure that anyone can reproduce the builds (to the byte!) that Parca distributes. That is a big vote of trust & confidence @brancz!

3. https://www.parca.dev/docs/kubernetes

Agent & server versions on the website are always in sync. It is re-generated in Vercel after a release gets created:
- https://github.com/parca-dev/parca/blob/7dc4a2456d95b124459fbc7661c9d9b9099f126d/.github/workflows/release.yml#L92-L94
- https://github.com/parca-dev/parca.dev/blame/da283aec395887e0bfff05d126897ef1e6b72323/docs/kubernetes.mdx#L89

title: 🎁 CI/CD Lego set
body:
## Why did we do this?
We needed an easy migration path between CircleCI and GitHub Actions, while developing the pipeline locally, and running a long blue-green experiment. One of the goals was to have a pipeline that is not written in YAML, and has as little vendor-specific boilerplate as possible. Think Docker, but for CI/CD.

We also wanted for any code change to be in production within 5 minutes. While our previous pipeline **appears** to take less than 5 minutes, it used to take 8-10 minutes when we started with this experiment. Because we have been running both pipelines in parallel, we can see exactly which one gets to production faster. Our new CI/CD pipeline is **at least** 2 minutes faster than the previous one. The reason why **at least** is important is because the time that CI jobs are waiting in the queue are not accounted for in the previous pipeline.

Previous pipeline:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/144934969-30d6a8cb-25bb-4472-87ca-2b4e2706dac0.png)

New pipeline:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/146631053-ae95e801-8724-4ad2-b78a-81d9a6e8bd5e.png)

## What happens inside the new pipeline?

```
                 app
                 |
                 v
test_db_start    deps ----------------------------------------\
|                |                      |                     |
|                v                      v                     v
|                deps_compile_test      deps_compile_prod     assets_compile
|                |                      |               |     |
|                |                      |               \-----|
|                v                      v                     |
\--------------> test                   image_prod_cache      assets_digest
                 |                      |                     |
test_db_stop <---|                      v                     |
                 |                      image_prod <----------/
                 |                      |
                 |                      v
                 \--------------------> image_prod_tag
```


## What makes the new pipeline better?

The new pipeline does the same thing as the previous one, and is ~2m quicker:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/145682942-6f214eb6-f502-4fb9-b099-10d3651c0285.png)

It will run the same against any Docker instance, including the local one 👍🏻

And OpenTracing is built-in 😎
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/145683021-29a040da-974b-470a-90d9-68c4e66cf11a.png)


## What does the GitHub Actions integration look like?

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/145105282-22a77cde-5a87-4db4-9547-95a7a9625f46.png)

Eyeballing the checks, this new approach is ~2x quicker than `build` which runs in CircleCI (1m vs 2m) and ~4x quicker than the initial GitHub Actions `mix test` implementation (1m vs 4m):
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/145105458-4835b3b5-a136-4e0e-aec4-83d02a3ff4cd.png)

And because the actual pipeline definition is not vendor-specific YAML, the GitHub Action definition is super simple. In other words, I can imagine YOUR_FAVOURITE_CI_HERE equivalent being just as simple:
```yaml
name: Prod image

on:
  push:
    branches:
  workflow_dispatch:

env:
  DOCKER_HOST: "tcp://100.113.182.91:2375"
  OTEL_EXPORTER_JAEGER_ENDPOINT: "http://100.113.182.91:14268/api/traces"

jobs:
  build_test_ship:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code...
        uses: actions/checkout@v2

      - name: Install Dagger...
        uses: dagger/dagger-action@v1
        with:
          # ⚠️  Keep this in sync with 2021/dagger.mk
          version: 0.1.0-alpha.31
          age-key: ${{ secrets.DAGGER_AGE_KEY }}
          args: version

      - name: Configure Tailscale tunnel for remote Docker Engine...
        uses: tailscale/github-action@v1
        with:
          authkey: ${{ secrets.TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY }}

      - name: Run prod_image environment with Dagger on remote Docker Engine...
        run: |
          /opt/hostedtoolcache/dagger/*/x64/dagger input text docker_host "$DOCKER_HOST" --environment prod_image
          /opt/hostedtoolcache/dagger/*/x64/dagger input text git_branch "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" --environment prod_image
          /opt/hostedtoolcache/dagger/*/x64/dagger input text git_sha "$GITHUB_SHA" --environment prod_image
          /opt/hostedtoolcache/dagger/*/x64/dagger input text git_author "$GITHUB_ACTOR" --environment prod_image
          /opt/hostedtoolcache/dagger/*/x64/dagger input text app_version "$(date -u +'%y.%-m.%-d+')$GITHUB_SHA" --environment prod_image
          /opt/hostedtoolcache/dagger/*/x64/dagger input text build_version "$(date -u +'%Y-%m-%dT%H.%M.%SZ')" --environment prod_image
          /opt/hostedtoolcache/dagger/*/x64/dagger input text build_url "$GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/actions/runs/$GITHUB_RUN_ID" --environment prod_image
          /opt/hostedtoolcache/dagger/*/x64/dagger up --environment prod_image --log-format plain
```

## Where can I find the "glue code" & new pipeline config?

- glue code [`2021/dagger.mk`](https://github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/pull/395/files#diff-9beaa194da9724432085b3b1afff0d77b0b0aecff8f73437ce01d9fff7fe07f2)
- new pipeline config [`2021/dagger/prod_image/main.cue`](https://github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/pull/395/files#diff-75636a2a7cf6d93c2c902a4e69088de187490dcfa601f54ec499652debc04ae6)

## What happens next?

- [x] Listen to @jlongtine & @grouville tell us more about this in [Ship It! #33](https://changelog.com/shipit/33)
- [x] Setup a managed Docker Engine (I'm thinking fly.io) OR integrate GitHub Actions cache with Dagger
- [ ] See if @shykes can break production. Seriously, check how Dagger "Europa" improves things

## So where is this CI/CD Lego set?

The Lego blocks that went into our new pipeline are already part of the [Dagger Universe](https://dagger.io). By the time we are finished, building/testing/shipping any Elixir or Phoenix app will be child's play. The changelog.com Phoenix app will be one way of assembling these Lego blocks, and we look forward to seeing your version of it. We are excited to use your improvements in our changelog.com CI/CD pipeline 🎁

## Should I read the comments below?

If you are curious about the steps that went into this, have a look, otherwise all the important details are above the fold, meaning in this top-level comment. This is it for now, have a great Christmas 2021 🎄

---

title: Expand Oban usage for logging, rerror reporting, and periodic jobs
body:
Hello!

Changelog switched to Oban a little while ago, and there were a few missing integrations and potential improvements I saw:

* Upgrade Oban to the recently released 2.8 to make use of the time unit syntax
* Unlock a variety of unused packages that aren't used anymore
* Use Oban's telemetry events for logging and error reporting to sentry
* Swap out Quantum for Oban to run periodic jobs (along with some refactoring to isolate individual runs)
* Make use of additions to the `Date` module rather than Timex and Timex.Interval

Thanks for all your news and podcasts; they're a definite favorite 💛

title: Optimizing N+1 index page queries
body:
This PR addresses the N+1 queries that are impacting the index page (and any subsequent paginated index pages).

Below are some images from the docker-compose prom+grafana PromEx metrics to quantify the results (the first hump is `master` branch, the second hump is this branch):

By removing the N+1 queries, less garbage collection events occur on the BEAM:
![Screenshot from 2021-03-07 15-18-43](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4753634/110253823-57196b80-7f5a-11eb-846d-59bbfcb8b6e8.png)

On localhost the Phoenix metrics are not impacted as much given that the DB and the app are on the same host so there is not a large penalty for network bound requests:
![Screenshot from 2021-03-07 15-19-54](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4753634/110253875-862fdd00-7f5a-11eb-9cfe-b070e0a99297.png)

This graph shows how many fewer DB operations are being performed per second. Across all the tables that are being accessed during the stress test, ~90,000 queries were being made per 30s time slice in `master` whereas in the current branch, ~12,000 queries were being made per 30s time slice. The average query time goes up slightly given the queries have joins now as opposed to fetching every related item thing one by one.
![Screenshot from 2021-03-07 15-19-33](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4753634/110253920-ba0b0280-7f5a-11eb-909f-9041b655dd79.png)

title: Run tests as circleci
body:
This should be merged after #257 

CircleCI runs tests in a container, based on thechangelog/runtime image, and uses the circleci/postgres:9.6 image for the db container. We need to be able to do the same locally so that if CircleCI is not available (regardless of the reason), changelog.com can carry on. Yes, things will be more inconvenient (no auto-triggers), but the world won't stop for changelog.com if CircleCI goes on holiday.

The end-goal is to be able to push changelog.com updates from local, old skool style. To be at ease with this approach, we must be able to go through the same process as CircleCI, including running tests.

title: Add make target for building & publishing runtime image
body:
Merge this before #258 

This is something that the Concourse does via the [`build-runtime` job](https://ci.changelog.com/teams/main/pipelines/changelog.com/jobs/build-runtime/builds/4). Since we want to replace Concourse with CircleCI, we'll need to be able to do this locally, with a single command.

The initial Dockerfile was stored in [infrastructure/roles/dotcom/files/docker/runtime/Dockerfile](https://github.com/thechangelog/infrastructure/blob/deef8db2f92becdcb796096d7077d683dd5ba3cb/roles/dotcom/files/docker/runtime/Dockerfile)
and in [changelog.com/Dockerfile](https://github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/blob/0611abb43f83792b7ff9e60ded0094ec0d6d5395/Dockerfile) since [#246](https://github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/pull/246). As of this story, `changelog.com/Dockerfile` will be split into multiple files: `Dockerfile.runtime` & `Dockerfile` which will build on `thechangelog/runtime`, an artefact of `Dockerfile.runtime`.

`thechangelog/runtime` image is used by [CircleCI for running tests](https://circleci.com/gh/thechangelog/changelog.com/240#tests/containers/0) (see the **Spin up Environment** output), and by docker-compose when [running the app locally](https://github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/blob/aa95d83f4dec757b2a7e0cc086253e16065bf8db/Makefile#L88-L95).

For the record, `Dockerfile.runtime` is the place where Elixir & Erlang used by changelog.com are updated. Elixir & Erlang versions are determined by `FROM circleci/elixir:1.6-node`. Since this image also includes **node.js**, we also pick up Yarn & others for asset compilation & digestion. The best part is that this image is maintained by CircleCI, so we will pick up any updates CircleCI does to this image by re-building it. Learn more about [Pre-Build CircleCI Docker Images](https://circleci.com/docs/2.0/circleci-images/).
